questions.text: The property of a metal by which it can be beaten into thin sheets is called:

key_points: Malleability is the property of metals to be beaten into thin sheets
rubric.expected_answer: (b) Malleability
rubric.hint: Think about which property lets metals be hammered flat without breaking.

questions.text:
(a) Explain the meanings of 'malleable' and 'ductile'. Give one example of each.
(b) Name the metal that is the most ductile.

key_points: Malleable: property of being beaten into thin sheets (e.g., gold, silver)
Ductile: property of being drawn into thin wires (e.g., gold, copper)
Gold is the most ductile metal; ~2 km wire from 1 g of gold
rubric.expected_answer: Malleable: metals that can be beaten into thin sheets (e.g., gold, silver). Ductile: metals that can be drawn into thin wires (e.g., gold). Gold is the most ductile metal.
rubric.hint: Connect each term to what changes shape: thin sheets versus thin wires.

questions.text: Carbon is a non-metal, yet graphite conducts electricity and diamond is the hardest natural substance. How do you explain these exceptions?

key_points: Graphite and diamond are allotropes of carbon
Graphite conducts electricity due to delocalized electrons in its layered structure
Diamond is the hardest natural substance due to its rigid tetrahedral lattice
These are exceptions to general non-metal properties
rubric.expected_answer: Carbon exists as allotropes. Graphite has delocalized electrons in its layered structure that allow electrical conduction. Diamond has a giant covalent lattice where all four valence electrons are used in bonding, making it extremely hard. These are exceptions to the general non-metallic property of being non-conductor and soft.
rubric.hint: Think about how atom arrangement in each allotrope determines its special behaviour.

questions.text: Which of the following metals reacts most vigorously with cold water, producing a flammable gas?

key_points: Potassium (and sodium) react vigorously with cold water to produce hydrogen gas
The reaction is so exothermic that hydrogen catches fire
2K + 2H₂O -> 2KOH + H₂
rubric.expected_answer: (c) Potassium
rubric.hint: Consider which metals sit right at the very top of the reactivity series.

questions.text: Hydrogen gas is NOT evolved when a metal reacts with which of the following acids?

key_points: HNO₃ is a strong oxidising agent
It oxidises H₂ produced to water
HNO₃ is itself reduced to nitrogen oxides (N₂O, NO, NO₂)
Exception: Mg and Mn react with very dilute HNO₃ to give H₂
rubric.expected_answer: (c) Dilute nitric acid — because HNO₃ is a strong oxidising agent that oxidises any H₂ formed to water.
rubric.hint: Think about what makes dilute nitric acid special compared to other dilute acids.

questions.text: Why is sodium metal stored immersed in kerosene oil? What would happen if it were exposed to air?

key_points: Sodium reacts vigorously with oxygen and moisture in air
The reaction is highly exothermic and can catch fire spontaneously
Kerosene prevents contact with air/water
4Na + O₂ -> 2Na₂O; 2Na + 2H₂O -> 2NaOH + H₂
rubric.expected_answer: Sodium reacts vigorously with oxygen and moisture in air, generating enough heat to catch fire. To prevent accidental fires and protect it from oxidation, sodium is stored immersed in kerosene oil.
rubric.hint: Focus on sodium reacting with both oxygen and moisture in air simultaneously.

questions.text:
Write balanced chemical equations for the following reactions:
(i) Iron reacts with steam.
(ii) Calcium reacts with water.
(iii) Magnesium reacts with hot water.

key_points: 3Fe(s) + 4H₂O(g) -> Fe₃O₄(s) + 4H₂(g)
Ca(s) + 2H₂O(l) -> Ca(OH)₂(aq) + H₂(g)
Mg(s) + 2H₂O(l) -> Mg(OH)₂(aq) + H₂(g)
Iron reacts only with steam; calcium floats due to H₂ bubbles sticking to surface
rubric.expected_answer:
(i) 3Fe(s) + 4H₂O(g) -> Fe₃O₄(s) + 4H₂(g)
(ii) Ca(s) + 2H₂O(l) -> Ca(OH)₂(aq) + H₂(g)
(iii) Mg(s) + 2H₂O(l) -> Mg(OH)₂(aq) + H₂(g)
rubric.hint: Apply the general metal plus water formula for each metal given the conditions.

questions.text:
Samples of four metals A, B, C and D were added to the following salt solutions:

| Metal | FeSO₄ | CuSO₄ | ZnSO₄ | AgNO₃ |
|-------|-------|-------|-------|-------|
| A | No reaction | Displacement | — | — |
| B | Displacement | No reaction | — | — |
| C | No reaction | No reaction | No reaction | Displacement |
| D | No reaction | No reaction | No reaction | No reaction |

(i) Which is the most reactive metal?
(ii) What would you observe if B is added to CuSO₄ solution?
(iii) Arrange metals A, B, C and D in decreasing order of reactivity.

key_points: B displaces Fe from FeSO₄ -> B is more reactive than Fe
A displaces Cu but not Fe -> Fe > A > Cu
C displaces Ag but not Cu -> Cu > C > Ag
D displaces nothing -> least reactive
Order: B > Fe > A > Cu > C > Ag > D
B is the most reactive
B in CuSO₄: blue colour fades, reddish copper deposits on B
rubric.expected_answer:
(i) B is the most reactive (displaces Fe from FeSO₄).
(ii) Blue colour of CuSO₄ fades; reddish copper deposits on metal B; B + CuSO₄ -> BSO₄ + Cu.
(iii) Decreasing reactivity: B > A > C > D (relative to known metals: B > Fe > A > Cu > C > Ag > D).
rubric.hint: A more reactive metal always displaces a less reactive one from its salt solution.

questions.text: What would you observe when zinc is added to a solution of iron(II) sulphate? Write the chemical equation for the reaction that takes place.

key_points: Zinc is more reactive than iron
Zinc displaces iron from FeSO₄ solution
Blue-green colour of FeSO₄ fades/becomes colourless
Grey iron deposits on zinc
Zn + FeSO₄ -> ZnSO₄ + Fe
rubric.expected_answer: Observation: The pale green colour of iron(II) sulphate solution fades and becomes colourless; a grey deposit of iron forms on the zinc. Equation: Zn(s) + FeSO₄(aq) -> ZnSO₄(aq) + Fe(s)
rubric.hint: Compare reactivity of Zn and Fe, then predict the colour change in solution.

questions.text:
Zinc reacts with dilute hydrochloric acid according to the equation:
Zn(s) + 2HCl(aq) -> ZnCl₂(aq) + H₂(g)
Calculate the number of moles of hydrogen gas produced when 13.0 g of zinc reacts completely with excess HCl. (Atomic mass of Zn = 65 u)

key_points: Molar mass of Zn = 65 g/mol
Moles of Zn = 13.0/65 = 0.2 mol
From equation: 1 mol Zn gives 1 mol H₂
Moles of H₂ = 0.2 mol
rubric.expected_answer: Moles of Zn = 13.0/65 = 0.20 mol. Since the molar ratio of Zn to H₂ is 1:1, moles of H₂ = 0.20 mol.
rubric.hint: Use moles equals mass over molar mass, then apply the 1:1 Zn:H2 ratio.

questions.text:
(a) What is the reactivity (activity) series of metals? List the metals K, Na, Ca, Mg, Al, Zn, Fe, Pb, Cu, Ag, Au in decreasing order of reactivity.
(b) Using the reactivity series, explain: (i) Why copper does not react with dilute H₂SO₄ but iron does. (ii) Why aluminium cannot be extracted from Al₂O₃ by heating with carbon. (iii) Write a displacement reaction involving iron and copper sulphate solution.

key_points: Reactivity series lists metals in decreasing order of reactivity: K>Na>Ca>Mg>Al>Zn>Fe>Pb>H>Cu>Hg>Ag>Au
Metals above H in series displace H from dilute acids; Cu is below H so no reaction
Metals below carbon in affinity for oxygen can be reduced by C; Al has more affinity for O than C, so carbon cannot reduce Al₂O₃
Fe + CuSO₄ -> FeSO₄ + Cu (Fe is more reactive than Cu)
rubric.expected_answer:
(a) The reactivity series lists metals in decreasing order of reactivity: K > Na > Ca > Mg > Al > Zn > Fe > Pb > [H] > Cu > Hg > Ag > Au.
(b)(i) Iron is above H in the series so it displaces H from dilute H₂SO₄: Fe + H₂SO₄ -> FeSO₄ + H₂. Copper is below H and cannot displace it.
(ii) Carbon can only reduce oxides of metals that are less reactive than carbon (below C in activity series). Aluminium is above carbon in reactivity/affinity for oxygen, so carbon cannot reduce Al₂O₃; electrolytic reduction is needed.
(iii) Fe(s) + CuSO₄(aq) -> FeSO₄(aq) + Cu(s)
rubric.hint: Anchor each explanation to where the metal sits relative to hydrogen in the series.

questions.text:
Assertion (A): Copper does not react with dilute sulphuric acid even on heating.
Reason (R): Copper is placed below hydrogen in the reactivity series.

Choose the correct option:
(a) Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
(b) Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
(c) A is true but R is false.
(d) A is false but R is true.

options.text: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

key_points: Copper is below hydrogen in the reactivity series
Metals below H cannot displace H from dilute acids
Therefore copper does not react with dilute H₂SO₄
R correctly explains A
rubric.expected_answer: (a) Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
rubric.hint: Decide if copper can displace hydrogen, and then check whether R correctly explains A.

questions.text:
Study Figure A showing two test tubes: (I) an iron nail placed in copper sulphate solution, and (II) a copper wire placed in iron sulphate solution.
(a) In which test tube does a reaction occur? What change do you observe?
(b) Write the balanced chemical equation for the reaction that takes place.
(c) What type of reaction is this? Name the principle illustrated.

key_points: Reaction occurs in Test tube I (iron nail in CuSO₄)
Blue colour of CuSO₄ fades; reddish copper deposits on iron nail
Fe(s) + CuSO₄(aq) -> FeSO₄(aq) + Cu(s)
Type: displacement (single displacement) reaction
Principle: more reactive metal displaces less reactive metal from its salt solution
rubric.expected_answer:
(a) Reaction occurs in Test tube I. Blue colour of CuSO₄ fades; reddish copper deposits on the iron nail.
(b) Fe(s) + CuSO₄(aq) -> FeSO₄(aq) + Cu(s)
(c) This is a displacement reaction. It illustrates that iron is more reactive than copper and displaces it from its salt solution.
rubric.hint: Ask which metal is more reactive and can displace the other from its salt solution.

questions.text:
A man dipped gold ornaments in a liquid and the ornaments sparkled but their weight reduced drastically.
(a) What is the nature of the liquid used?
(b) Write its composition and ratio.
(c) Why can this liquid dissolve gold when neither of its components can do so alone?

key_points: The liquid is aqua regia (Latin: 'royal water')
Composed of conc. HCl : conc. HNO₃ in ratio 3:1
HNO₃ oxidises gold to Au³⁺ ions; HCl provides Cl⁻ ions that form stable AuCl₄⁻ complex
The synergistic action of the two acids dissolves gold; neither acid alone can do so
Aqua regia is highly corrosive and fuming
rubric.expected_answer:
(a) The liquid is aqua regia (highly corrosive, fuming liquid).
(b) Aqua regia is a freshly prepared mixture of conc. HCl and conc. HNO₃ in ratio 3:1.
(c) HNO₃ acts as an oxidising agent to oxidise gold, while HCl provides chloride ions that form the stable tetrachloroaurate complex (AuCl₄⁻), keeping Au in solution. Neither acid alone creates both conditions simultaneously.
rubric.hint: Think about a famous acid mixture that dissolves gold by combining oxidising and complexing roles.

questions.text: Ionic compounds conduct electricity in the molten state but NOT in the solid state because:

options.text: Solid ionic compounds have no ions
In molten state, ions are free to move; in solid state, ions are held in rigid lattice
Solid ionic compounds are insoluble in water

key_points: In solid state, ions are held in fixed positions by strong electrostatic forces
In molten state, heat overcomes electrostatic forces and ions become mobile
Mobile ions carry charge -> electricity conducted
rubric.expected_answer: (b) In the solid state, ions are locked in a rigid crystal lattice and cannot move. On melting, ions become free to migrate and conduct electricity.
rubric.hint: Focus on whether ions can move freely in each state to carry charge.

questions.text:
(i) Write the electron-dot structures for sodium and oxygen.
(ii) Show the formation of Na₂O by the transfer of electrons.
(iii) Name the ions present in Na₂O.

key_points: Na has 1 electron in outermost shell (2,8,1); O has 6 electrons (2,6)
Two Na atoms each donate 1 electron to one O atom
Na⁺ (2,8) and O²⁻ (2,8) are formed
Na₂O contains Na⁺ (sodium cation) and O²⁻ (oxide anion)
rubric.expected_answer:
(i) Na: [Na]· (one dot); O: ·[O]·· (six dots arranged in pairs)
(ii) Two Na atoms each lose one electron -> 2 Na⁺. One O atom gains two electrons -> O²⁻. Na₂O is formed by electrostatic attraction.
(iii) Ions in Na₂O: Na⁺ (sodium cation) and O²⁻ (oxide anion).
rubric.hint: Track electron transfer step by step: Na gives electrons, O receives them.

questions.text: Why do ionic compounds have high melting and boiling points?

key_points: Ionic compounds consist of oppositely charged ions held together by strong electrostatic forces
A large amount of energy is required to overcome these inter-ionic forces
Therefore they have high melting and boiling points (e.g., NaCl: mp 1074 K)
rubric.expected_answer: Ionic compounds have high melting and boiling points because they consist of oppositely charged ions held together by strong electrostatic forces of attraction. A considerable amount of energy is required to break these strong inter-ionic attractions, resulting in high melting and boiling points.
rubric.hint: Think about the strength of electrostatic forces between oppositely charged ions in the lattice.

questions.text: Ionic compounds conduct electricity in aqueous solution and in the molten state, but not in the solid state. Explain with reference to the movement of ions.

key_points: In solid state: ions are in fixed positions in the crystal lattice; cannot move -> no conduction
In aqueous solution: water molecules dissociate the lattice; free ions migrate to electrodes -> conduction
In molten state: heat breaks the lattice; ions are free to migrate -> conduction
Conduction requires movement of charged particles
rubric.expected_answer: In solid state, ions occupy fixed positions in the rigid crystal lattice and cannot migrate, so no electrical conduction. In aqueous solution, the ionic lattice dissociates; positive ions move to cathode and negative ions to anode, carrying charge. In the molten state, the heat energy overcomes the electrostatic forces, freeing ions to move and conduct electricity.
rubric.hint: Consider whether ions can migrate in each state; migration is required for conduction.

questions.text:
(a) Explain the formation of sodium chloride (NaCl) and magnesium chloride (MgCl₂) by transfer of electrons. Draw electron-dot diagrams for both.
(b) List any three general properties of ionic compounds.
(c) An ionic compound X has a melting point of 1074 K and is soluble in water. Identify X.

key_points: NaCl: Na (2,8,1) loses 1e⁻ -> Na⁺; Cl (2,8,7) gains 1e⁻ -> Cl⁻
MgCl₂: Mg (2,8,2) loses 2e⁻ -> Mg²⁺; 2 Cl atoms each gain 1e⁻ -> 2Cl⁻
Ionic compounds: (i) solid and hard due to strong electrostatic forces (ii) high MP/BP (iii) soluble in water, insoluble in organic solvents (iv) conduct electricity in molten/dissolved state
X = NaCl (mp 1074 K from Table 3.4)
rubric.expected_answer:
(a) NaCl: Na donates 1 electron to Cl; Na⁺ and Cl⁻ form. MgCl₂: Mg donates 2 electrons (1 each) to 2 Cl atoms; Mg²⁺ and 2Cl⁻ form.
(b) Properties: (i) Ionic compounds are solids, hard and brittle; (ii) They have high melting and boiling points; (iii) They are generally soluble in water and conduct electricity in solution/molten state.
(c) X = NaCl (sodium chloride), which has a melting point of 1074 K.
rubric.hint: Trace how electrons move from each metal atom to chloride ions during bond formation.

questions.text: Which of the following statements about ionic compounds is INCORRECT?

options.text: Ionic compounds are generally brittle and break under pressure
Ionic compounds in solid state do not conduct electricity
Ionic compounds are generally insoluble in water but soluble in kerosene
Ionic compounds have higher melting points than most covalent compounds

key_points: Ionic compounds are SOLUBLE in water and INSOLUBLE in organic solvents like kerosene
Option C reverses this — it is incorrect
All other options are correct properties of ionic compounds
rubric.expected_answer: (c) Ionic compounds are generally SOLUBLE in water and INSOLUBLE in organic solvents like kerosene. Statement C reverses this and is incorrect.
rubric.hint: Recall whether ionic compounds dissolve in water or in non-polar organic solvents.

questions.text: The process of converting sulphide ores into oxides by heating strongly in the presence of excess air is called:

key_points: Roasting: heating sulphide ores in excess air -> metal oxide + SO₂
Calcination: heating carbonate ores in limited air -> metal oxide + CO₂
2ZnS + 3O₂ -> 2ZnO + 2SO₂ (roasting example)
rubric.expected_answer: (c) Roasting
rubric.hint: Distinguish between ore type (sulphide vs carbonate) and the type of air supply used.

questions.text: In the electrolytic refining of copper, which of the following is correct?

options.text: Impure copper is the cathode; pure copper is the anode
Impure copper is the anode; pure copper is the cathode
Both electrodes are made of impure copper

key_points: Anode = impure metal (dissolves into electrolyte)
Cathode = thin strip of pure metal (pure metal deposits here)
Electrolyte = solution of the metal's salt (acidified CuSO₄)
Insoluble impurities settle as anode mud
rubric.expected_answer: (b) Impure copper is the anode; pure copper is the cathode.
rubric.hint: Remember which electrode is impure and which one accumulates pure deposited metal.

questions.text: Distinguish between calcination and roasting. Give one chemical equation for each process using zinc ores as examples.

key_points: Calcination: heating carbonate ores in limited/absence of air -> metal oxide + CO₂
Roasting: heating sulphide ores in excess air -> metal oxide + SO₂
Calcination of ZnCO₃: ZnCO₃ -> ZnO + CO₂
Roasting of ZnS: 2ZnS + 3O₂ -> 2ZnO + 2SO₂
rubric.expected_answer:
Calcination: Heating carbonate ores in limited/absence of air to form the metal oxide and carbon dioxide. ZnCO₃(s) -> ZnO(s) + CO₂(g)
Roasting: Heating sulphide ores in excess air to form the metal oxide and sulphur dioxide. 2ZnS(s) + 3O₂(g) -> 2ZnO(s) + 2SO₂(g)
rubric.hint: Focus on ore type, air supply, and the gas released for each process.

questions.text:
Define the following terms with examples:
(i) Mineral
(ii) Ore
(iii) Gangue

key_points: Mineral: elements or compounds that occur naturally in the earth's crust
Ore: minerals containing a very high percentage of a particular metal from which the metal can be profitably extracted
Gangue: impurities (soil, sand, etc.) present in the ore along with the metal compound
rubric.expected_answer:
(i) Mineral: Elements or compounds that occur naturally in the earth's crust. E.g., haematite (Fe₂O₃), bauxite (Al₂O₃).
(ii) Ore: A mineral from which a metal can be profitably extracted. E.g., haematite is an ore of iron.
(iii) Gangue: Unwanted rocky and earthly impurities (such as sand, soil) mixed with the ore. Gangue must be removed before extraction.
rubric.hint: Each term describes a different category: natural occurrence, usefulness, and impurity.

questions.text:
Copper is found as Cu₂S in nature.
(i) Write the chemical equations for extraction of copper from Cu₂S.
(ii) How is impure copper then refined? Name the process.

key_points: Step 1: 2Cu₂S + 3O₂ -> 2Cu₂O + 2SO₂ (roasting)
Step 2: 2Cu₂O + Cu₂S -> 6Cu + SO₂ (smelting)
Impure copper refined by electrolytic refining
Impure Cu = anode; pure Cu = cathode; CuSO₄ solution = electrolyte
rubric.expected_answer:
(i) Step 1 (roasting): 2Cu₂S(s) + 3O₂(g) -> 2Cu₂O(s) + 2SO₂(g)
Step 2 (smelting): 2Cu₂O(s) + Cu₂S(s) -> 6Cu(s) + SO₂(g)
(ii) Electrolytic refining: impure Cu is the anode, pure Cu strip is the cathode, and acidified CuSO₄ solution is the electrolyte. Pure Cu deposits at cathode; impurities settle as anode mud.
rubric.hint: Cu2S is a sulphide ore; think roasting, then smelting, then electrolytic purification.

questions.text:
(i) What is the thermite reaction? Write the balanced chemical equation.
(ii) State one important industrial application of the thermite reaction.
(iii) Identify the substance oxidised and the substance reduced in the thermite reaction.

key_points: Thermite reaction: Fe₂O₃ + 2Al -> 2Fe(l) + Al₂O₃ + Heat
Highly exothermic displacement reaction; iron produced in molten state
Application: welding railway tracks or cracked machine parts
Al is oxidised (loses electrons, Al→Al³⁺); Fe₂O₃ is reduced (Fe³⁺→Fe)
rubric.expected_answer:
(i) Thermite reaction: the highly exothermic reaction of iron(III) oxide with aluminium powder, producing molten iron and aluminium oxide. Fe₂O₃(s) + 2Al(s) -> 2Fe(l) + Al₂O₃(s) + Heat
(ii) Application: joining railway tracks or repairing cracked machine parts (thermite welding).
(iii) Al is oxidised (Al -> Al³⁺); Fe in Fe₂O₃ is reduced (Fe³⁺ -> Fe).
rubric.hint: Identify which substance gains oxygen and which loses it, then link to the application.

questions.text:
In the electrolytic refining of copper, 6.4 g of copper dissolves from the impure anode and an equivalent amount is deposited at the pure cathode.
(a) How many moles of Cu dissolve from the anode? (Atomic mass of Cu = 64 u)
(b) Write the ionic equations at the anode and cathode.
(c) If the same mass of zinc (At. mass = 65 u) were used instead, how many moles would dissolve?

key_points: Moles of Cu = 6.4/64 = 0.1 mol
At anode: Cu -> Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ (oxidation)
At cathode: Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ -> Cu (reduction)
Moles of Zn = 6.4/65 ≈ 0.098 mol
rubric.expected_answer:
(a) Moles of Cu = 6.4/64 = 0.10 mol
(b) Anode: Cu(s) -> Cu²⁺(aq) + 2e⁻; Cathode: Cu²⁺(aq) + 2e⁻ -> Cu(s)
(c) Moles of Zn = 6.4/65 ≈ 0.098 mol ≈ 0.10 mol
rubric.hint: Apply moles equals mass divided by molar mass, then write the electrode half-reactions.

questions.text:
Study Figure A showing the electrolytic refining of copper.
(a) Identify the electrodes labelled A (left) and B (right). Which one is the anode?
(b) What is the composition of the electrolyte?
(c) What are 'anode mud' particles? Give two examples of metals found in anode mud.

key_points: A (left) = impure copper = anode
B (right) = pure copper strip = cathode
Electrolyte = acidified copper sulphate solution
Anode mud = insoluble impurities that settle below anode when anode dissolves
Examples: gold, silver (precious metal impurities)
rubric.expected_answer:
(a) A = impure copper (anode); B = pure copper strip (cathode). A is the anode.
(b) Electrolyte = acidified copper sulphate (CuSO₄) solution.
(c) Anode mud consists of insoluble impurities that settle at the bottom as the impure anode dissolves. Examples: gold and silver.
rubric.hint: The impure electrode dissolves; insoluble impurities settle below it as anode mud.

questions.text:
Assertion (A): Carbon cannot be used to reduce the oxides of sodium, magnesium, calcium and aluminium.
Reason (R): These metals have a greater affinity for oxygen than carbon has.

(a) Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
(b) Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
(c) A is true but R is false.
(d) A is false but R is true.

options.text: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

key_points: Na, Mg, Ca, Al are at top of reactivity series
These metals have more affinity for oxygen than carbon
Carbon cannot displace them from their oxides
They are extracted by electrolytic reduction instead
rubric.expected_answer: (a) Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
rubric.hint: Consider whether these metals cling to oxygen more strongly than carbon does.

questions.text:
(a) Gold is found in the free (native) state in nature, but sodium is found only in the combined state. Explain why.
(b) Give the position of gold and sodium in the reactivity series and state the method used to extract sodium from its ore.

key_points: Gold is at the bottom of the activity series — least reactive
It does not react with oxygen, water, or acids under normal conditions -> found in free state
Sodium is at the top of the activity series — most reactive
It reacts vigorously with oxygen and water -> only found as compounds (NaCl, Na₂SO₄, etc.)
Sodium is extracted by electrolysis of molten NaCl
At cathode: Na⁺ + e⁻ -> Na; At anode: 2Cl⁻ -> Cl₂ + 2e⁻
rubric.expected_answer:
(a) Gold is at the bottom of the reactivity series and is very unreactive; it does not react with oxygen, water, or common acids, so it occurs in the free/native state. Sodium is extremely reactive (top of series), readily reacts with oxygen and water, and is therefore found only in combined form as ores like NaCl.
(b) Gold: bottom of series (least reactive). Sodium: top of series (most reactive). Sodium is extracted by electrolysis of molten sodium chloride (NaCl). At cathode: Na⁺ + e⁻ -> Na; At anode: 2Cl⁻ -> Cl₂ + 2e⁻.
rubric.hint: Link reactivity series position to whether a metal occurs free or combined.

questions.text: The process of coating iron or steel with a thin layer of zinc to prevent rusting is called:

key_points: Galvanisation = coating iron/steel with zinc
Zinc acts as a sacrificial metal: being more reactive, it corrodes preferentially
Protects iron even if zinc coating is damaged
rubric.expected_answer: (b) Galvanisation
rubric.hint: Think about which metal acts sacrificially, being more reactive than iron.

questions.text:
(a) What is galvanisation?
(b) The galvanised article is protected against rusting even if the zinc coating is broken. Explain why.

key_points: Galvanisation: method of coating iron/steel with zinc to prevent rusting
Even if zinc coating breaks, zinc (more reactive than iron) acts as a sacrificial anode
Zinc corrodes preferentially, protecting iron from oxidation
This is the principle of sacrificial protection or cathodic protection
rubric.expected_answer:
(a) Galvanisation is the process of coating iron or steel with a thin layer of zinc to prevent rusting.
(b) Zinc is more reactive than iron. Even if the zinc coating is broken, zinc acts as a sacrificial metal — it corrodes preferentially (oxidises first), protecting the exposed iron from rusting. This is called sacrificial protection.
rubric.hint: Zinc is more reactive than iron; consider what happens when zinc corrodes preferentially.

questions.text:
Pure gold is known as 24-carat gold. In India, 22-carat gold is commonly used for making jewellery.
(a) Calculate the percentage of pure gold in 22-carat gold.
(b) Calculate the mass of pure gold in a 22-carat gold ornament that weighs 48 g.
(c) What is the remaining 2 parts made of, and why?

key_points: Mass of pure gold = (22/24) × 48 = 44 g
Remaining 2 parts = copper or silver (to make gold harder for jewellery use)
24-carat gold is too soft for making jewellery
rubric.expected_answer:
(a) % of pure gold = (22/24) × 100 = 91.67%
(b) Mass of pure gold = (22/24) × 48 = 44 g
(c) Remaining 2 parts = copper or silver. Pure (24-carat) gold is very soft and not suitable for jewellery; alloying makes it harder and more durable.
rubric.hint: Use the fraction carat divided by 24 to find the proportion of pure gold.

questions.text:
Explain how metals in the middle of the activity series (such as Zn, Fe, Pb, Cu) are extracted from their ores.
(a) Why are these metals generally found as sulphide or carbonate ores?
(b) Write equations for roasting of zinc sulphide and calcination of zinc carbonate.
(c) How is the metal oxide then reduced to the metal? Write the equation for reduction of ZnO with carbon.
(d) Iron cannot be extracted from its oxide by reduction with carbon in all cases. Describe the thermite reaction and state one practical application.

key_points: Middle activity series metals: Zn, Fe, Pb, Cu — found as sulphides (ZnS, PbS, Cu2S) or carbonates (ZnCO3, FeCO3) because these are stable forms
Roasting (sulphide -> oxide): 2ZnS + 3O2 -> 2ZnO + 2SO2
Calcination (carbonate -> oxide): ZnCO3 -> ZnO + CO2
Reduction of oxide with carbon: ZnO + C -> Zn + CO (at high temp)
Thermite reaction: Fe2O3 + 2Al -> Al2O3 + 2Fe + heat; Al is more reactive, displaces Fe
Application: welding of railway tracks (thermite welding)
rubric.expected_answer:
(a) Sulphide/carbonate ores: middle series metals are moderately reactive; they react with S and CO3 in the earth's crust to form stable sulphide and carbonate ores.
(b) Roasting: 2ZnS + 3O2 -> 2ZnO + 2SO2 (heated in excess air)
    Calcination: ZnCO3 -> ZnO + CO2 (heated in absence of air)
(c) Reduction: ZnO + C -> Zn + CO (at high temperature). Carbon (coke) acts as reducing agent.
(d) Thermite reaction: Fe2O3 + 2Al -> Al2O3 + 2Fe + heat. Aluminium (more reactive) reduces iron oxide. Used for thermite welding of cracked railway tracks.
rubric.hint: Link ore type to extraction: sulphide or carbonate becomes oxide first, then reduced.

questions.text:
(a) Describe Activity 3.14 (experiment to find conditions required for rusting of iron). What conclusions can you draw from this experiment?
(b) Explain why platinum, gold and silver are used for making jewellery.
(c) An iron pillar in Delhi has not rusted for over 1600 years. What does this suggest about ancient Indian metallurgy?
(d) List any three methods used to prevent corrosion of metals.

key_points: Activity 3.14: three test tubes — A (air + water -> rusts), B (water, no air -> no rust), C (dry air, no water -> no rust)
Conclusion: both air (oxygen) and water are necessary for rusting
Pt, Au, Ag: very unreactive (at bottom of activity series); resist corrosion, maintain lustre
Iron pillar: ancient Indian metallurgists had mastered low-corrosion iron (possibly due to phosphorus content creating protective layer)
Prevention methods: painting, oiling, galvanising, anodising, alloying, chrome plating
rubric.expected_answer:
(a) Three test tubes with iron nails: A — air + water (rusts); B — boiled water + oil layer, no air (no rust); C — dry air, no water (no rust). Conclusion: both moisture and oxygen are simultaneously required for rusting.
(b) Pt, Au, Ag are at the bottom of the reactivity series and do not react with oxygen, water, or common chemicals; they maintain lustre and do not corrode.
(c) It suggests that ancient Indian iron workers had developed metallurgical techniques to produce iron with exceptional corrosion resistance (possibly through high phosphorus content or other alloying method).
(d) Painting, galvanising, alloying (e.g., stainless steel), anodising (any 3).
rubric.hint: Focus on the two simultaneous conditions needed for rusting and why noble metals resist it.

questions.text: The property of metals that produces a ringing sound when struck with a hard object is called:

key_points: Sonority: property of producing sound when struck
School bells made of metals because of sonority
rubric.expected_answer: (c) Sonority
rubric.hint: Think about which physical property involves metals producing sound when struck.

questions.text: Which of the following metals is a liquid at room temperature?

key_points: Mercury is the only metal liquid at room temperature
rubric.expected_answer: (b) Mercury
rubric.hint: Recall which single metal is uniquely liquid at room temperature.

questions.text: Electric wires have a coating of PVC or rubber. Give two reasons why metals are used for the wire core, and one reason why the coating is necessary.

key_points: Metals: good conductors + ductile (drawn into wires)
PVC is insulator — prevents electric shock/short circuits
rubric.expected_answer: Metals: excellent conductors; ductile. PVC coating is insulator preventing shocks.
rubric.hint: Think about conductivity and ductility for the core, and insulation for the coating.

questions.text: When a metal reacts with water, the products formed are:

key_points: Metal + Water -> Metal oxide + H₂
rubric.expected_answer: (a) Metal oxide and hydrogen
rubric.hint: Recall the two general products formed when any metal reacts with water.

questions.text: Which metal reacts with steam but does NOT react with cold or hot water?

key_points: 3Fe + 4H₂O(steam) -> Fe₃O₄ + 4H₂
Iron does not react with cold or hot water
rubric.expected_answer: (c) Iron
rubric.hint: Think about which metal reacts only with steam, not cold or hot water.

questions.text: A copper wire is placed in iron(II) sulphate solution. After 20 minutes, what is observed?

options.text: Blue colour develops; iron deposits on copper
No reaction; solution and wire unchanged
Green colour fades; copper deposits on wire

key_points: Copper less reactive than iron; cannot displace Fe from FeSO₄
rubric.expected_answer: (b) No reaction
rubric.hint: Apply the reactivity series: can a less reactive metal displace a more reactive one?

questions.text: Write balanced equations for: (i) Aluminium with steam. (ii) Iron with steam. (iii) Sodium with cold water.

key_points: 2Al + 3H₂O -> Al₂O₃ + 3H₂
3Fe + 4H₂O -> Fe₃O₄ + 4H₂
2Na + 2H₂O -> 2NaOH + H₂
rubric.expected_answer: (i) 2Al(s)+3H₂O(g)->Al₂O₃(s)+3H₂(g) (ii) 3Fe(s)+4H₂O(g)->Fe₃O₄(s)+4H₂(g) (iii) 2Na(s)+2H₂O(l)->2NaOH(aq)+H₂(g)
rubric.hint: Each metal reacts differently; write the oxide or hydroxide product based on reactivity.

questions.text: (a) Name the gas produced when zinc reacts with dilute H₂SO₄. (b) Write the balanced equation. (c) How is this gas tested?

key_points: Zn + H₂SO₄ -> ZnSO₄ + H₂
Test: burning splint gives pop sound
rubric.expected_answer: (a) Hydrogen. (b) Zn(s)+H₂SO₄(aq)->ZnSO₄(aq)+H₂(g). (c) Burning splint: pop sound.
rubric.hint: Think about the gas produced when metals react with dilute acids and its flame test.

questions.text: Magnesium does not react with cold water but reacts with hot water and vigorously with steam. Explain the trend.

key_points: Mg has moderate reactivity
Cold: insufficient energy; hot water -> Mg(OH)₂+H₂; steam -> MgO+H₂
rubric.expected_answer: Mg moderate reactivity. Cold: no reaction. Hot water: Mg+2H₂O->Mg(OH)₂+H₂. Steam (higher T): vigorous, MgO+H₂.
rubric.hint: Higher temperature supplies more energy; trace how the product changes from hot water to steam.

questions.text: Fe(s) + 2HCl(aq) -> FeCl₂(aq) + H₂(g). (a) Moles of H₂ from 28 g Fe (At. mass Fe=56). (b) Mass of FeCl₂ produced (M=127 g/mol).

key_points: moles Fe=28/56=0.5
moles H₂=0.5
mass FeCl₂=0.5×127=63.5 g
rubric.expected_answer: (a) 0.5 mol H₂. (b) 63.5 g FeCl₂
rubric.hint: Divide mass of Fe by its molar mass, then use the 1:1 ratio for FeCl2.

questions.text:
Metals Zn, Al, Fe, Mg and Cu were tested with water. Mg reacts with hot water/steam; Al, Fe, Zn react only with steam; Cu shows no reaction.
(i) Arrange in decreasing reactivity. (ii) Which react with dilute HCl? Write one equation.

key_points: Decreasing: Mg > Al≈Zn≈Fe > Cu
All except Cu react with dilute HCl
Zn+2HCl->ZnCl₂+H₂
rubric.expected_answer: (i) Mg > Al≈Zn≈Fe > Cu (ii) Mg, Al, Zn, Fe react. Eq: Zn(s)+2HCl(aq)->ZnCl₂(aq)+H₂(g)
rubric.hint: Rank metals by their water reactivity, then identify which sit above hydrogen in the series.

questions.text: Hydrogen gas is NOT evolved when a metal reacts with dilute HNO₃ because:

options.text: HNO₃ does not react with metals
HNO₃ is a strong oxidising agent that oxidises H₂ to water
Metals below H do not react with HNO₃

key_points: HNO₃ oxidises H₂ produced to H₂O; reduced to N₂O/NO/NO₂
rubric.expected_answer: (b) HNO₃ is a strong oxidising agent that oxidises H₂ to water.
rubric.hint: Think about what makes nitric acid an oxidising agent, not just an acid.

questions.text: Ionic compounds in solid state do not conduct electricity because:

options.text: Ions are fixed in the crystal lattice and cannot move
They are insoluble in all solvents

key_points: Ions in fixed positions; no movement -> no conduction
rubric.expected_answer: (b) Ions are fixed in crystal lattice and cannot move.
rubric.hint: Ask whether ions can physically move in a rigid crystal lattice.

questions.text: Which is an ionic compound formed by electron transfer?

key_points: NaCl: Na donates 1e to Cl
H₂O/CO₂/HCl are covalent
rubric.expected_answer: (c) NaCl
rubric.hint: Consider which compound is formed by electron transfer rather than electron sharing.

questions.text: Show the formation of NaCl by electron transfer using electron-dot diagrams. Explain why NaCl does not exist as discrete molecules.

key_points: NaCl = aggregate of ions in crystal lattice, not molecules
rubric.expected_answer: Na loses 1e to Cl forming Na⁺ and Cl⁻. Held by electrostatic attraction. NaCl exists as crystal lattice aggregate, not discrete molecules.
rubric.hint: Show electron configurations before and after transfer; Na loses one, Cl gains one.

questions.text: Ionic compounds are hard but brittle. Explain both properties in terms of ion arrangement.

key_points: Hard: strong electrostatic forces resist deformation
Brittle: pressure shifts planes; like charges align -> repulsion shatters crystal
rubric.expected_answer: Hard: strong electrostatic attraction resists deformation. Brittle: pressure shifts layers, like charges align, repulsion shatters crystal.
rubric.hint: Strong forces resist deformation; shifted planes align like charges causing repulsion.

questions.text: 2.4 g of Mg burns in O₂ forming MgO. (a) Write balanced equation. (b) Moles of MgO formed (At. mass Mg=24, O=16). (c) Mass of MgO produced.

key_points: 2Mg+O₂->2MgO
mass MgO=0.1×40=4.0 g
rubric.expected_answer: (a) 2Mg+O₂->2MgO (b) 0.1 mol (c) 4.0 g
rubric.hint: Divide mass of Mg by its molar mass; the 1:1 ratio gives moles of MgO.

questions.text: In electrolytic refining, pure metal deposits at the:

key_points: Cathode: Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ -> Cu (pure)
rubric.expected_answer: (b) Cathode
rubric.hint: Think about where in the electrolytic cell metal ions are reduced to metal atoms.

questions.text: Highly reactive metals (Na, Mg, Ca) are extracted by:

key_points: Carbon cannot reduce these; electrolysis of molten chlorides used
rubric.expected_answer: (c) Electrolytic reduction of molten salts
rubric.hint: Consider whether carbon can displace a metal that bonds more strongly with oxygen.

questions.text: Define with examples: (i) Mineral (ii) Ore (iii) Gangue

key_points: Mineral: naturally occurring compound in earth's crust
Ore: mineral from which metal profitably extracted
Gangue: earthy impurities in ore
rubric.expected_answer: (i) Mineral: naturally occurring in earth's crust, e.g. haematite. (ii) Ore: mineral for profitable extraction, e.g. bauxite. (iii) Gangue: earthy impurities in ore, e.g. sand.
rubric.hint: Distinguish between natural occurrence, profitable extraction, and unwanted impurity.

questions.text: Why is it easier to reduce a metal oxide than its sulphide or carbonate? What pre-treatment is needed for sulphide and carbonate ores?

key_points: Oxides directly reduced by coke
Sulphides roasted to oxide; carbonates calcined to oxide first
rubric.expected_answer: Oxides reduced directly by carbon. Sulphides -> roasting -> oxide. Carbonates -> calcination -> oxide. Then reduced.
rubric.hint: Think about which form of an ore can be directly reduced by carbon without pre-treatment.

questions.text: Write balanced equations for: (i) Roasting ZnS (ii) Calcination ZnCO₃ (iii) Reduction of ZnO with carbon

key_points: 2ZnS+3O₂->2ZnO+2SO₂
ZnCO₃->ZnO+CO₂
ZnO+C->Zn+CO
rubric.expected_answer: (i) 2ZnS(s)+3O₂(g)->2ZnO(s)+2SO₂(g) (ii) ZnCO₃(s)->ZnO(s)+CO₂(g) (iii) ZnO(s)+C(s)->Zn(s)+CO(g)
rubric.hint: Write each step: ore to oxide conversion, then oxide to metal reduction equation.

questions.text: (a) What is anode mud? (b) Why do Au and Ag collect as anode mud in copper refining? (c) Why is electrolytic refining economically important?

key_points: Anode mud = insoluble impurities below anode
Au/Ag less reactive than Cu; do not dissolve in CuSO₄
Economic: pure Cu higher value; Au/Ag recovered
rubric.expected_answer: (a) Insoluble impurities below anode. (b) Au/Ag less reactive than Cu; do not ionise in CuSO₄. (c) Pure Cu has higher value; Au/Ag from anode mud give extra revenue.
rubric.hint: Consider why less reactive metals like Au and Ag do not dissolve into the electrolyte.

questions.text:
19.2 g of copper deposits at cathode during electrolytic refining (At. mass Cu=64).
(a) Moles of Cu? (b) Moles of electrons transferred (Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ -> Cu)? (c) Write the cathode half-reaction.

key_points: Cu²⁺(aq)+2e⁻->Cu(s)
rubric.expected_answer: (a) 0.3 mol (b) 0.6 mol (c) Cu²⁺(aq)+2e⁻->Cu(s)
rubric.hint: Divide mass by molar mass for Cu; each Cu2+ ion requires 2 electrons.

questions.text: Carbon cannot reduce oxides of Na, Mg, Al, Ca because:

options.text: These metals do not form oxides
Carbon reacts with the metals directly
These metals have greater affinity for oxygen than carbon
Carbon does not react with metal oxides

key_points: Na/Mg/Al/Ca bond more strongly with O₂ than carbon
Their oxides more stable than CO/CO₂
rubric.expected_answer: (c) These metals have greater affinity for oxygen than carbon.
rubric.hint: Compare which element holds oxygen more tightly: carbon or these highly reactive metals.

questions.text: Copper vessels gain a green coat on prolonged exposure to moist air. The green substance is:

key_points: Cu reacts with moist CO₂ in air -> Cu₂(OH)₂CO₃
rubric.expected_answer: (c) Basic copper carbonate Cu₂(OH)₂CO₃
rubric.hint: Think about what copper forms when it reacts with moist CO2 in air.

questions.text: State two conditions necessary for rusting of iron. How does Activity 3.14 demonstrate these conditions?

key_points: Conditions: moisture AND oxygen (both required)
Tube A (air+water)->rusts; Tube B (water, no air)->no rust; Tube C (dry air)->no rust
rubric.expected_answer: Conditions: moisture + oxygen. Tube A rusts; B and C do not. Both required simultaneously.
rubric.hint: Compare test tubes: which had both air and water versus only one condition.

questions.text:
(a) Aluminium is highly reactive yet used for cooking utensils. Explain.
(b) Tarnished copper cleaned with lemon/tamarind juice. Explain why.

key_points: Al quickly forms impervious Al₂O₃ layer; prevents further corrosion
Lemon/tamarind acidic; dissolves Cu₂(OH)₂CO₃; restores shine
rubric.expected_answer: (a) Al forms impervious Al₂O₃ layer — self-protecting. (b) Acid in lemon/tamarind dissolves green Cu₂(OH)₂CO₃ coating.
rubric.hint: Think about Al forming a protective oxide and acid in lemon dissolving copper tarnish.

questions.text:
22-carat gold = 22 parts gold + 2 parts copper in 24.
(a) Calculate % pure gold. (b) Mass of gold in 12 g bangle. (c) Compare with 18-carat: which has more gold?

key_points: 18-carat: 75%; 22-carat has more gold
rubric.expected_answer: (a) 91.67% (b) 11.0 g (c) 18-carat=75%; 22-carat has more pure gold
rubric.hint: Use carat divided by 24 times 100 for percentage, then scale to find the mass.
